title: Aladdin and His Wonderful Lamp
byline: Popeye Color Special cartoon directed by Dave Fleischer and produced by Max Fleischer, released April 7, 1939.

evidence.note: Wikipedia says this short and the other two Popeye Color Specials are in the public domain. That is a secondary claim, not a primary record.
evidence.source: Wikipedia article: Aladdin and His Wonderful Lamp

evidence.note: The Catalog of Copyright Entries, Motion Pictures, 1966, 1967 and 1968 volumes were fetched and scanned through a text-extraction tool for the renewal sections. No renewal entry for this title, for Popeye, or for Max Fleischer was reported in any of them. The tool read the volumes in excerpts and did not cover every page, so this is not a complete, verifiable renewal search. The Copyright Office public catalog was not searched. Treat the result as not proven either way.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Motion Pictures, 1967 (archive.org)

evidence.note: Wikipedia credits the music to Sammy Timberg (infobox: music by Sammy Timberg; text: music supervised by Sammy Timberg). This is a sound film, so the recorded track would normally share the print's status, but the print's status is not confirmed.
evidence.source: Wikipedia article: Aladdin and His Wonderful Lamp

evidence.note: Wikipedia says this short and the other two Popeye Color Specials are adapted from One Thousand and One Nights, a centuries-old tale collection. The source is not copyrightable in the US. The Popeye character is separate and is not covered by this finding.
evidence.source: Wikipedia article: Aladdin and His Wonderful Lamp

editorial:
Aladdin and His Wonderful Lamp is the last of the three Popeye Color Specials. Dave Fleischer directed it, Max Fleischer produced it, and Paramount distributed it on April 7, 1939, as a two-reel Technicolor short from Fleischer Studios. Sammy Timberg is credited for the music and Jack Mercer voices Popeye. A creator would want it for the colour Fleischer animation and a recognisable cast in a story taken from One Thousand and One Nights.

The rights trap is that the print's status is not yet proven here. Wikipedia calls the short public domain, but the renewal check is incomplete: the 1966, 1967 and 1968 Catalog of Copyright Entries volumes were only scanned in excerpts, and no renewal entry was reported, which does not prove none exists. The Copyright Office catalog was not searched. Do not rely on the print until you have run those searches yourself. Separately, the Aladdin tale is free, but the Popeye character and any franchise marks are a distinct question that this dossier leaves undetermined.
faq: Is this Popeye cartoon free to reuse?

Not yet confirmed here. Wikipedia describes it as public domain, but the renewal search of the 1966-1968 catalogs was partial and no Copyright Office record was checked. Run those searches before you reuse it.
Does the Aladdin story being old make the cartoon free?
It frees the underlying tale from One Thousand and One Nights. It does not settle the film's own copyright, the music track, or any rights in the Popeye character.
